chapter: New Orleans second line and Armstrong
title: Robinson, kids playing along in parades, and Sister Kate
summary: He explains Robinson's advice against clarinet, says he saw no kids playing with bands except Armstrong's kazoo-like instrument, and discusses Sister Kate.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: You could hear them for miles. Did you ever play a little Ken flute or anything?

No, nothing, no Ken or anything. And I didn't, I told my mom, I said I don't want to play this, I said I want to play a clarinet. So she told Mr. Robinson, she says, his name was William Robinson, she said he don't want to play the trombone, he wants the clarinet. And so he told me, he says, listen, a good trombone player can always find work. Well it's just the reverse now. Was that in Chicago or New Orleans when you got here on? That was in Chicago. I didn't even touch yesterday on New Orleans.
Well did any of the kids when they went on those parades, did they ever play any little Ken flute or anything with the other band in the second line?
The only first time I saw anybody playing a thing like that was Louis Armstrong.
He had one of them, you know the slide. You mean the kids didn't play along with the band in the street or anything?

I never saw any, I never saw any of them. Once I heard that they did. Singling and whistling, you know it was a great whistling time. It's good for singing and whistling. Like all them tunes like Sister Kate by Rack, that's Louis Armstrong's tune. That's the same. I don't want to get in no trouble. No, Louis told me that and Natty Dominick said that he wrote on.
Well I heard that before I ever come down.
That tune I heard it before it came from New Orleans.
